reconcile.connective: Gill reads Isaiah's 'perisheth' as bodily death only, not the eternal ruin that would cancel Psalm 92's promise of flourishing.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the plain wording, filing Psalm 92:12's flourishing against Isaiah 57:1's unnoticed perishing as flatly opposed answers to one question.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Will the righteous flourish?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/flourish.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/flourish.html

excerpts.excerpt_text: Not eternally … but he cannot perish everlastingly, because he is one that believes in Christ, and is justified by his righteousness, from whence he is denominated righteous; and such shall never perish, but have everlasting life: but the meaning is, that he perisheth as to his outward man, or dies corporeally, which is called perishing …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly explains why 'the righteous perisheth' (Isa 57:1) does not cancel Psalm 92:12's promise of flourishing: Gill reads the 'perishing' as bodily death only, set against an eternal life the righteous can never lose.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats Isaiah 57:1 ('the righteous perisheth') directly, tabling it opposite the wicked's 'perish' texts to show both use the same Hebrew term (abadh) and arguing the word cannot bear the annihilationist weight some readers put on it — i.e., 'perisheth' need not mean the righteous's final ruin (Examination, pp. 204-205).
